summary: No direct evidence on a Democratic Eisenhower exists. Sources show Truman's offers and Eisenhower's refusal, and give 1952 group voting patterns (Southern whites, Black voters, women) as analogues. Eisenhower's appeal rested on distance from an unpopular 20-year Democratic record.

notes:
I found direct evidence on Eisenhower's own stance and on how groups voted in 1952. I found nothing reliable for your third question or for the exact "loyal share" figures in your second. The sources below are mostly student theses, Wikipedia and a foundation site, so treat everything as provisional.

**1. Direct evidence**

- **Eisenhower's stance.** Truman privately offered in 1948 to run as Eisenhower's vice-president on a Democratic ticket. Truman proposed that the two run together on the Democratic ticket, with Eisenhower as the presidential candidate. [S6] Eisenhower rejected the offer.
- **The 1951 letter.** Just before Christmas 1951, a letter from President Truman arrived offering his support if Ike would run as a Democrat. [S1] Eisenhower declined, and he told Lodge that he considered himself a Republican [S4].
- **His reasons.** One account says he believed he would win more easily, with a larger congressional majority, as a Democrat, but felt the Truman administration had become corrupt [S4]. This comes from Wikipedia and needs checking against Pickett's 2000 book, *Eisenhower Decides To Run*.
- **Ideology.** Clark Clifford's memoir, as quoted in a forum thread (so unreliable), says Eisenhower disagreed with much of the New Deal and Fair Deal. I could not verify this.
- **Why the scenario matters.** Truman's approval had fallen to 23%, the lowest of any president since approval polling began [S4]. Eisenhower's value came from being unconnected to the Democratic record, with many Democrats wanting change after 20 years of Democratic control of the White House [S5]. As a Democrat he would have lost that distance from the incumbent record. I found no scholarly estimate of the net effect on turnout or vote share.

**2. Analogues: how groups actually voted in 1952**

These show how groups behaved when party label and personal appeal conflicted, with Eisenhower as the Republican. They are not direct evidence of loyalty to a Democratic Eisenhower.

- **Overall.** Eisenhower won 55.18% of the popular vote to Stevenson's 44.33%. [S10] He carried every state outside the South. [S13]
- **Who shifted.** Republicans gained among Democrats, especially urban and suburban Southerners, and white ethnic groups in the Northeast and Midwest. [S10]
- **South, whites.** Eisenhower won 50 percent of the votes cast by southern whites in 1952, plus Florida, Virginia, Texas and Tennessee. [S7] That is notable because only one in nine Southern voters was a registered Republican [S7].
- **South, urban and suburban.** Republican gains came from the growing cities and suburbs of the peripheral South. [S7] Southern Democratic leaders also split. South Carolina Governor Byrnes and Virginia Senator Harry Byrd refused to support the Democratic ticket. [S7]
- **Black voters.** Stevenson outperformed Eisenhower among Black voters. [S9] A Gallup figure reported in a student thesis put Eisenhower's 1952 share at 21%, rising to 42% in 1956 [S8]. In the same thesis, Gallup put Democratic strength among African Americans falling from 72% to 56% between October 1952 and September 1956 [S8]. Lubell's study of Black wards in 86 cities, in the same source, put Eisenhower's 1956 share at 36 percent [S8].
- **Gender.** Women were five percent more likely to vote for Eisenhower than men, though both gave him a majority. [S11] That gap was 6% in 1956 [S11].
- **Groups with no evidence.** I found nothing on naturalized immigrants, non-citizens, or Midwest, Northeast, West and border states as separate groups. Non-citizens could not vote.

**Your three questions**

- **War-hero admirers by party loyalty in 1952.** I found no reliable breakdown. The only measure of defection I found is the Southern white figure above, and it applies to Eisenhower as a Republican.
- **Share of Southern and urban Democrats who would have stayed loyal.** I found no figure. Southern Democrats loyal to the label would likely have stayed, but nothing I found measures that. Another unmeasured factor is how many Republican-leaning voters Eisenhower would have lost.
- **Personal vote following a war hero who changed party.** I found nothing reliable and did not search the cases from memory. Candidates to research are Taylor, Grant and MacArthur, but I have no evidence on any of them.

**3. Named people**

- **Truman.** He offered the vice-presidency in 1947 or 1948, per the sources above, and wrote to Eisenhower in December 1951.
- **Eisenhower.** His reply was "I do not feel that I have any duty to seek a political nomination." [S4] On October 14, 1951, he wrote a confidential letter to supporters saying he would run if drafted at the Republican convention. [S1] In early January 1952 his campaign announced that he was a Republican. [S1]
- **Stevenson.** He dismissed reports of Southern defections and expected to hold Texas, Louisiana and Florida [S7].

**4. Limits**

- **Real Eisenhower, not the hypothetical.** The 1952 swings measure Eisenhower against a Democratic successor to an unpopular administration. A Democratic Eisenhower would have removed the "time for a change" appeal, and might have split the Democratic organisation or Republican voters.
- **Southern whites.** Their 1952 shift was tied to the Dixiecrat revolt of 1948, the Tidelands issue and civil rights. Those factors would not simply reverse under a Democratic Eisenhower.
- **Black voters.** The 1956 numbers come from a different election and may include the effect of his civil rights record.
- **Source quality.** The group-level figures come from student theses and secondary summaries, not primary survey data such as the Michigan SRC 1952 study. A proper answer needs those.
prompt:
Scenario for the 1952 United States presidential election (election day 1952-11-04).
A reader asked: "Dwight Eisenhower runs for president as a Democrat in 1952.".
As modelled: The famous general seeks the presidency under the banner of the party in office since 1933 instead of the party out of the presidency since 1933.
Kind of change: issue. Populations it reaches first: every voter.
Include how the same groups swung, by how much, when comparable issues or shocks hit nearby elections.

Questions to answer:
- How did voters who admired the general as a war hero split by party loyalty in 1952 when party labels and personal popularity conflicted?
- In 1952 how many Southern and urban voters of the party in office since 1933 would have stayed loyal to a candidate of their own party who was a famous nonpartisan figure?
- In similar elections where a popular war hero changed party, how much of his personal vote followed him?

Groups the simulation distinguishes: men and women; native-born white, naturalized immigrant, non-citizen immigrant and Black adults; the Northeast, Midwest, South (the eleven former Confederate states), border states and West. Evidence by these groups is most useful.
